text:
British philosophy - Wikipedia
Contents
British philosophy
British philosophy
refers to the
philosophical
tradition of the
British people
, a part of
British culture
. The universities of
Oxford
and
Cambridge
both have long philosophical traditions since
medieval times
.
British philosophy includes medieval philosophers like
Saint Anselm of Canterbury
,
Duns Scotus
, and
William of Ockham
, and includes modern philosophers and schools such as
Francis Bacon
,
Thomas Hobbes
, the
British empiricists
,
utilitarians
, and
British idealists
. Since the 20th century, British philosophy has been dominated by
analytic philosophy
.
Characterizations
According to one author "The native characteristics of British philosophy are these:
common sense
, dislike of complication, a strong preference for the
concrete over the abstract
and a certain awkward honesty of method in which an occasional pearl of
poetry
is embedded".
[
1
]
According to American pragmatist
Charles Sanders Peirce
: "From very early times, it has been the chief intellectual characteristics of the English to wish to effect everything by the plainest and directest means, without unnecessary contrivance...In philosophy, this national tendency appears as a strong preference for the simplest theories, and a resistance to any complication of the theory as long as there is the least possibility that the facts can be explained in the simpler way. And, accordingly, British philosophers have always desired to weed out of philosophy all conceptions which could not be made perfectly definite and easily intelligible, and have shown strong
nominalistic
tendencies since the time of
Edward I
, or even earlier."
[
2
]
Bertrand Russell
wrote: "The British are distinguished among the nations of modern Europe, on the one hand by the excellence of their philosophers, and on the other hand by their contempt for philosophy. In both respects they show their wisdom."
[
3
]
Medieval
Medieval philosophy
was very much a part of
Christian philosophy
and
theology
. It was also much concerned with the
problem of universals
, inherited from
antiquity
.
The
Old English Boethius
translation was attributed in one manuscript to
King Alfred
(r. 870–899), and this was long accepted, but the attribution is now considered doubtful.
[
4
]
The Roman
neoplatonist
Boethius
wrote
The Consolation of Philosophy
(524) and influenced philosophy with his dictum to "join faith to reason".
[
5
]
John Scotus Erigena
(
c.
800
–c. 877) was a mystical neoplatonist from
Ireland
, who translated and made commentaries upon the work of
Pseudo Dionysius the Areopagite
. He succeeded
Charlemagne
's scholar
Alcuin of York
(c. 735–804) as head of the Palace School at
Aachen
.
Bertrand Russell
dubbed him "the most astonishing person of the
ninth century
".
[
6
]
The
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
states that "He is generally recognized to be both the outstanding philosopher (in terms of originality) of the
Carolingian era
and of the whole period of
Latin
philosophy stretching from
Boethius
to
Anselm
".
[
7
]
Saint
Anselm of Canterbury
(c. 1033–1109) held the office of
Archbishop of Canterbury
from 1093 to 1109. Anselm is best known as the originator of the
ontological argument
for the existence of God and the satisfaction theory of atonement, found in the
Proslogion
(c. 1078).
[
8
]
Before Canterbury, Anselm was at the French
abbey of Bec
. The followers of
William the Conqueror
supported the abbey, enriching it with extensive properties in
England
following the
Battle of Hastings
in 1066.
[
9
]
[
a
]
Adelard of Bath
(
c.
1080
–
c.
1150) may be the first philosopher from England. He is best known as the translator of
Euclid
's
Elements
,
and also was one of the first to introduce the
Arabic numeral system
to Europe.
[
13
]
He also translated the
astronomical
tables of
al-Khwarizmi
.
Robert of Chester
also translated al-Khwarizmi.
[
14
]
Adelard was a follower of French philosopher
Walter of Mortagne
(c. 1100–1174),
[
15
]
leader of the "indifferentists", a type of platonist who attempts to avoid the more extreme forms of platonism, and according to whom the universal it itself indifferent, changing according to points of view.
[
16
]
John of Salisbury
(late 1110s–1180) was one of the most notable figures of the
twelfth century Renaissance
during the
High Middle Ages
.
[
17
]
He was made
Bishop of Chartres
and advocated
Cicero
's
academic skepticism
.
[
18
]
John of Salisbury wrote the
Policraticus
(c. 1159) and the
Metalogicon
.
[
17
]
Daniel of Morley
(c. 1140–c. 1210) and
Michael Scot
(c. 1175–c. 1232) traveled to Toledo, known for its
school of translators
of
Greek and Arabic sources
, which included
Alfred of Sareshel
.
[
19
]
Michael Scot translated Aristotle, Avicenna, and
Averroes
, and was the greatest public intellectual of his day.
[
20
]
The University of Oxford goes back as far as 1096, and grew rapidly after 1167, when King
Henry II
temporarily prohibited students from attending the
University of Paris
.
[
21
]
After conflicts between students and townspeople, some Oxford academics fled northeast and established the University of Cambridge in 1209.
[
22
]
The two universities share much in common and are jointly referred to as
Oxbridge
.
[
23
]
John Blund
(c. 1175–1248) taught at Oxford alongside
Edmund of Abingdon
(c. 1174–1240). Blund is called by medieval historian
Maurice Powicke
the "first English Aristotelian."
[
24
]
Blund wrote
Tractatus de Anima
(c. 1200), one of the first western philosophy works to make use of the recently translated
De Anima
by
Aristotle
, and also
Avicenna
's work on the soul, also called
De Anima
.
[
25
]
Alexander Neckam
(1157–1217), an abbot of
Cirencester Abbey
who taught at Oxford, was influenced by Blund.
[
25
]
According to one author, he was one of the first Western scholars to know the translations of Aristotle,
[
26
]
but he was also interested in Platonism. In his
Speculum speculationum
(c. 1215), Alexander combats the
Cathar heresy
, particularly its belief in
dualism
, and applies
dialectic logic
to the study of theology.
[
27
]
He also contributed the earliest European description of the
compass
.
[
28
]
Oxford's
Adam of Bockenfield
(c. 1220–1293) and
Richard Rufus of Cornwall
(d. c. 1260) also wrote on Aristotle.
[
29
]
Alexander of Hales
(c. 1185–1245) given the
scholastic
accolade
of
Doctor Irrefragibilis
(Latin: "Irrefutable Teacher") introduced
Peter Lombard
's
Sentences
(c. 1150) as the textbook at the
University of Paris
.
[
30
]
He believed in
free will
, and became a
Franciscan
, "edifying the world and giving new status to the Order."
[
31
]
Robert Grosseteste
(
c.
1170
–
1253) played a key role in the development of
science
.
A.
C. Crombie
called him "the real founder of the tradition of scientific thought in medieval
Oxford
, and in some ways, of the modern English intellectual tradition".
[
32
]
Grosseteste studied
optics
and believed in the "metaphysics of light", identifying
light
with Aristotelian
form
, writing such works as
On Light
.
[
33
]
[
b
]
A friend of Grosseteste was
Adam Marsh
(
c.
1200
–1259).
[
34
]
Oxford's
Richard Fishacre
(c. 1200–1248) was influenced by Grosseteste, and wrote a commentary of
Sentences
.
[
35
]
Bartholomaeus Anglicus
(1202–1272) is also believed to have studied under Grosseteste.
[
36
]
William of Sherwood
(c. 1200
–
1272) was an English
logician
and teacher. Little is known of his life, but he is thought to have studied in
Paris
and was a master at
Oxford
in 1252. He was the author of two books which were an important influence on the development of
scholastic
terminist
logic in both Britain and on the continent:
Introduction to Logic
and
Syncategoremata
. These are the first known works about what is now called
supposition theory
.
[
c
]
Syncategoremata
were terms like "and", "or", and "not" which merely combine other terms, while
categoremata
could genuinely act as
predicates
.
[
38
]
A treatise on "insolubles" or
paradoxes
like the
Liar Paradox
was also attributed to William of Sherwood.
[
39
]
[
40
]
Roger Bacon
(c. 1214–1294), also known as
Doctor Mirabilis
(Latin: "Wondrous Doctor"), was an English
Franciscan
friar, who commented on Aristotle, Avicenna, and
Averroes
.
[
41
]
His views are found in works like the
Opus Majus
,
Opus Minus
, and
Opus Tertium
(1267).
[
42
]
Roger Bacon was highly influenced by Aristotle's
Metaphysics
, but his view on universals is debated among scholars, and so is resolved as "both ‘extreme-realism’ and proto-nominalism".
[
41
]
He also wrote
The Art and Science of Logic,
[
42
]
and is the great British contributor to Aristotle's logic of the period, along with William of Sherwood.
[
43
]
Roger Bacon was influenced by Grosseteste and Marsh. He studied optics,
astronomy
, and
alchemy
, and is credited as an early advocate of science.
[
44
]
[
45
]
[
46
]
He was the first European to describe
gunpowder
, and also proposed
early flying machines
like
hot-air balloons
and an
ornithopter
.
[
47
]
Roger Bacon influenced
John Peckham
(c. 1230– 1292), who taught
Roger Marston
(d. c. 1303).
[
42
]
[
48
]
John Duns Scotus
(c. 1265–1308) also known as
Doctor Subtilis
(Latin: "the subtle doctor") was from
Duns
, in
Berwickshire
,
Scotland
.
[
49
]
In 1291 he was ordained as a priest in
Northampton
,
England
. A note in Codex 66 of
Merton College, Oxford
, records that Scotus "flourished at
Cambridge
,
Oxford
and
Paris
". He was
beatified
by
Pope John Paul II
.
[
50
]
Scotus is well known for the
univocity of being
, the
formal distinction
, and the idea of
haecceity
.
[
51
]
The
Scotist
view of the univocity of being holds that existence is the most abstract concept we have and is applicable to everything that exists. It is contrasted with the
Thomist
view of the equivocity of being and
analogia entis
. The British Thomists included
William of Hotham
,
Richard of Clapwell
, and
Thomas of Sutton
.
[
52
]
The formal distinction is a distinction that is intermediate between a merely conceptual distinction, and a logical distinction that is fully real or mind-independent.
[
53
]
Haecceity is the idea of "thisness," a concept which denotes the discrete qualities, properties or characteristics of a thing which make it a particular thing.
[
54
]
Thomas Wilton
studied under Scotus.
[
55
]
Walter Burley
(c. 1275–1345) studied under Wilton. Burley was a noted logician.
[
56
]
Thomas Bradwardine
(c. 1300–1349) was a follower of Scotus who with
Richard Swineshead
(fl. c. 1340–1354),
William Heytesbury
(c. 1313–1373) , and
John Dumbleton
(c. 1310–1349) formed the
Oxford Calculators
, who were influenced by Burley.
[
57
]
[
58
]
As well as using logic in philosophical and theological disputes, they studied mathematics and physics. Influenced by French thinkers
Gerard of Brussels
and
Nicole Oresme
, they studied
acceleration
or "uniform difform motion."
[
59
]
William of Ockham
(c. 1288–c. 1348) was an
English
Franciscan
friar
and
scholastic
philosopher
. Ockham advocated
nominalism
as a solution to the
problem of universals
in such works as
Summa Logicae
(1323).
[
60
]
He is perhaps best known for his principle of parsimony, famously known as
Ockham's razor
. This actual term is claimed not to appear in his writings,
[
61
]
but rather summarizes the principle he expressed in passages such as
Plurality must never be posited without necessity
[
62
]
[
63
]
and
It is futile to do with more things that which can be done with fewer
.
[
64
]
[
d
]
Generally it refers to distinguishing between two hypotheses, with the metaphor of a razor used either by "shaving away" unnecessary assumptions or cutting apart two similar conclusions.
[
67
]
Ockham had followers like
Robert Holcot
(c. 1290–1349),
Adam of Wodeham
(1298–1358), and
William Crathorn
(fl. c. 1330). Holcot was known as the
Doctor firmus et indefatigabilis
(Latin: "strong and tireless doctor") and died of the
Black plague
.
[
68
]
Walter Chatton
(c. 1290–1343) was Ockham's intellectual rival.
[
69
]
Crathorn and Chatton both criticized Aristotelian notions of space.
[
70
]
Ockham's followers influenced
Pelagians
like
Thomas of Buckingham
and
Uthred of Boldon
(c. 1320–1397).
[
58
]
[
71
]
Ockham spent his final years taking refuge with
Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor
at the
Alter Hof
in
Munich
, and his work also influenced
French
and
German philosophy
.
[
72
]
John Wycliffe
(1328–1384) was one of the last scholastics, and an important predecessor of
Protestantism
.
[
73
]
Wycliffe led the
Lollards
, who were opposed by scholastic
Reginald Pecock
(c. 1395–c. 1461), who was influenced by Holcot.
[
74
]
German
Reformation
pioneer
Martin Luther
accepted in his
Assertio
that Wycliffe taught that "all events occur by absolute
necessity
."
[
75
]
[
e
]
Hermit
Richard Rolle
(c. 1300–1349) was a mystic, whose disciple was
anchoress
Margaret Kirkby
(c. 1322–c. 1392).
[
77
]
Another mystic was the anonymous Neoplatonist author of
The Cloud of Unknowing
.
[
78
]
There were also anchoress
Julian of Norwich
(c. 1343–c. 1418), author of
Revelations of Divine Love
, and
Walter Hilton
(c. 1340–1396).
[
78
]
Modern
Renaissance humanist
Thomas More
(1478–1535) wrote
Utopia
(1516), which describes the
political system
of an
imaginary
island state.
[
79
]
More opposed the Protestant Reformation and
separation from the Catholic Church
by King
Henry VIII
, who
dissolved
the
monasteries
. More was convicted of treason and beheaded at
Tower Hill
.
Pope Pius XI
canonised More in 1935 as a martyr.
[
80
]
Anglican
John Jewel
(1522–1571) influenced
Richard Hooker
(1554–1600), a Thomist who believed the world was governed by
natural law
.
[
81
]
His defense of redeemed
reason
informed the theology of the
Caroline Divines
.
[
82
]
There were British Renaissance logicians like
Thomas Wilson
,
Ralph Lever
,
John Seton
,
John Sanderson
, and
Richard Crakanthorpe
. Thomas Wilson (1524–1581) wrote
Logique
(1551)
[
83
]
and
The Arte of Rhetorique
(1553),
[
84
]
which have been called "the first complete works on
logic
and
rhetoric
in English".
[
85
]
Ralph Lever (d. c. 1585) wrote
The Arte of Reason, rightly termed, Witcraft
(1573). The work of John Seton (c. 1498–1567) and John Sanderson (d. 1602) joined Wilson as the standard texts on logic for nearly a century.
[
86
]
[
87
]
Richard Crakanthorpe (1567–1624) is alluded to in the novel
Tristram Shandy
.
[
88
]
At Cambridge,
William Temple
(1555–1627) defended French logician, educational reformer, and Protestant convert
Petrus Ramus
against the attacks of Aristotelian and Neoplatonist
Everard Digby
(c. 1550–c. 1592).
[
71
]
According to historian
Thomas Fuller
, nobody was "better skilled in Aristotle or a greater follower of Ramus" than
George Downame
(c. 1566—1634).
[
89
]
Downame influenced
Paradise Lost
(1667) author
John Milton
(1608–1674), who also wrote
Art of Logic
(1672).
[
90
]
[
91
]
[
92
]
Another
Ramist
was
William Ames
(1576–1633), especially influential in
New England
and
Colonial America
.
[
93
]
Digby influenced mystic
Robert Fludd
(1574–1637) and Neoplatonist
Robert Greville
(1607–1643), a
Parliamentarian
general in the
English Civil War
(1642–1651) killed by a
Royalist
sniper at the
Siege of Lichfield
.
[
71
]
English dissenter
John Pordage
(1607–1681) was inspired by German
theosophist
Jakob Böhme
.
[
94
]
In 1694, Pordage adherent and
universalist
visionary
Jane Leade
(1624–1704), who wrote the spiritual diary
A Fountain of Gardens
, founded the
Philadelphian Society
for the Advancement of Piety and Divine Philosophy.
[
95
]
[
f
]
The Philadelphian Society included physician
Francis Lee
, Parliamentarian
Roger Crab
, prophet
Ann Bathurst
, and clergyman
Richard Roach
.
[
96
]
Mysticism influenced the
antinomian
Ranters
,
[
97
]
who influenced
George Fox
(1624–1691), founder of
Quakerism
.
[
98
]
William Law
(1686–1761) was an influential mystic.
[
99
]
So was poet
William Blake
(1757–1827).
[
100
]
Francis Bacon
(1561–1626) served both as
Attorney General
and
Lord Chancellor
of England. Although his political career ended in disgrace, he remained very influential through his philosophical works.
[
101
]
Francis Bacon was a pivotal figure in the
Scientific Revolution
and has been called the father of
empiricism
, the view that knowledge comes from the
senses
.
[
102
]
In works like
The Advancement of Learning
(1605) and
Novum Organum
(1620), Francis Bacon argued against Aristotelian approaches to logic and science (the old
Organon
). He rejected pure
a priori
deduction
, instead demanding
experiment
, and so established and popularized
inductive
methodology
. This is often called the
Baconian method
or simply, the
scientific method
.
[
103
]
Quoting him, "Nature to be commanded must be obeyed."
[
104
]
His dedication to experiment probably led to his death. He contracted
pneumonia
while stuffing a fowl with snow, in order to study the effects of freezing on the preservation of meat.
[
105
]
His posthumously published
New Atlantis
(1626) presents his vision of the future.
The
Royal Society
was founded in 1660, when twelve natural philosophers influenced by Bacon's philosophy met at
Gresham College
, starting a "Colledge for the Promoting of Physico-Mathematicall Experimentall Learning".
[
106
]
Remarkably it included both Parliamentarians (
Robert Boyle
,
John Wilkins
,
William Petty
,
Jonathan Goddard
, and
Abraham Hill
) and Royalists (
William Ball
,
William Brouncker
,
Alexander Bruce, 2nd Earl of Kincardine
,
Christopher Wren
,
Robert Moray
, and
Sir Paul Neile
).
[
107
]
Lawrence Rooke
alludes classification.
[
108
]
Bacon's philosophy also influenced predecessor institutions like
Gresham College
and the
Invisible College
. Shortly after the end of the
First English Civil War
, John Wilkins (1614–1672) wrote
Mathematicall Magick
(1648), and then moved to Oxford, where Wilkins started the
Oxford Philosophical Club
, active from 1649 to 1660.
[
109
]
Not to be confused with the Oxford Philosophical Society, which
Robert Plot
(1640–1696) started in 1683 at the
Ashmolean Museum
.
[
110
]
Wilkins was
Oliver Cromwell
's brother-in-law.
[
111
]
William Petty (1623–1687) travelled with Cromwell's
army in Ireland
as physician-general and is best known for his work on early
economics
.
[
112
]
Jonathan Goddard (1617–1675) was also a physician for Cromwell, one of those attending to him at his death.
[
113
]
Alexander Bruce (1629–1681) served as a captain with the Royalist cavalry, fighting at the
Battle of Worcester
.
[
114
]
Robert Boyle (1627–1691) wrote
The Sceptical Chymist
(1661) and is considered one of the founders of modern
chemistry
. He is the namesake of
Boyle's law
. Boyle rejected the
scholastic
hylomorphism
inherited from Aristotle. He also criticized German hermeticist and
alchemist
Paracelsus
.
[
115
]
In 1662, Parliamentarian
Henry Oldenburg
(c. 1618–1677) became secretary of the Royal Society.
[
116
]
Royalist
Walter Charleton
(1619–1707) joined in 1663. Charleton followed French
Epicurean
Pierre Gassendi
and was "the main conduit for the transmission of Epicurean ideas to England".
[
117
]
John Evelyn
(1620–1706) was another Royalist who joined in 1663, best known for his
diary
.
[
118
]
The Royal Society's journal
Philosophical Transactions
was established in 1665.
[
119
]
Christopher Wren (1632–1723) is best known for his architecture done in the
English Baroque
style after the
Great Fire of London
(1666), which came soon after the
Great Plague
(1665-1666). Wren rebuilt
52 churches
including
St Paul's Cathedral
.
[
120
]
[
121
]
Wren was also a natural philosopher. His friend
Robert Hooke
(1635–1703) commented: "Since the time of
Archimedes
there scarce ever met in one man in so great perfection such a mechanical hand and so philosophical mind."
[
122
]
Thomas Hobbes
(1588–1679) was an English philosopher, remembered today for his work on
political philosophy
. His book
Leviathan
(1651) established
social contract
theory.
[
123
]
Hobbes argued for a
sovereign
absolute monarch
to save man from the
state of nature
wherein life was "solitary, poor,
nasty, brutish, and short
".
[
124
]
Although Hobbes was a champion of monarchy, he also developed some of the fundamentals of European
liberal
thought: the
right
of the individual; the natural
equality
of all men; the artificial character of the political order (which led to the later distinction between
civil society
and the state); the view that all legitimate political power must be "representative" and based on the
consent of the people
; and a liberal interpretation of law which leaves people free to do whatever the law does not explicitly forbid.
[
125
]
Hobbes was a
materialist
, a
nominalist
, and an
egoist
, who had an intellectual rivalry with French philosopher and "founder of modern philosophy" and
Cartesianism
René Descartes
(1596–1650).
[
126
]
Hobbes influenced
Bernard Mandeville
(1670–1733), author of
The Fable of the Bees
(1714).
[
127
]
As well as philosophy, Hobbes contributed to a diverse array of fields, including
geometry
,
[
128
]
[
129
]
the physics of
gases
,
history
, and
anthropology
.
[
130
]
His debate with Boyle is traced in
Leviathan and the Air-Pump
(1985). He also
debated
mathematician
John Wallis
.
[
131
]
The
Cambridge Platonists
like
Benjamin Whichcote
,
Ralph Cudworth
, and
Henry More
, were an influential group of Neoplatonists.
[
132
]
They influenced the likes of
Peter Sterry
,
Nathanael Culverwel
,
Joseph Glanvill
,
Richard Cumberland
,
Anne Conway
,
George Rust
,
John Smith
, and
John Norris
.
[
133
]
Benjamin Whichcote (1609– 1683) disagreed with
total depravity
. He was also a Platonist who called reason "the very voice of God."
[
134
]
Ralph Cudworth (1617– 1688) was a leading opponent of Hobbes, known for his
The True Intellectual System of the Universe
(1678).
[
135
]
Cudworth challenged Hobbes' determinism, believing in free will and a
hegemonikon
or command center of the mind and soul connecting it to the body, a notion borrowed from the
Stoics
.
[
136
]
Henry More (1614–1687) was a leading critic of Descartes and Cartesianism. More rejected
Cartesian dualism
, arguing that spirit, like matter, must be
extended
in space. He coined the term
fourth dimension
and introduced the concept of

156
]
Locke held to

in the

, believing all of the objects of the understanding are ideas, where ideas exist in the mind. One of his goals in his work

157
]
While there are innate capacities for Locke,
[
158
]
there are no
innate ideas

159
]

160
]

Primary qualities are thought to be

sensations

,
taste
,
smell
, and
sound

161

Simple

concepts
